objectives: Apply energy-deficit principles and BMI to obesity, and carbohydrate counting and glycemic control to type-2 diabetes.
Explain cardiovascular nutrition (sodium and lipids) and core sports-nutrition strategies (carbohydrate loading, protein timing, hydration, creatine).
Distinguish enteral from parenteral nutrition support and recognize the nutritional features of eating disorders.

slides.title: Clinical nutrition: obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease
slides.body:
**Clinical nutrition** applies nutritional science to the prevention and treatment of disease. Three conditions dominate practice in industrialized nations: obesity, type-2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.

**Obesity** is excess body fat sufficient to harm health. The standard population screen is the **body mass index (BMI)**, devised by the Belgian statistician **Adolphe Quetelet** in the 1830s (originally the *Quetelet Index*):

$$\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{weight (kg)}}{[\text{height (m)}]^2}$$

The **World Health Organization** classifies BMI **18.5–24.9 as normal**, **25–29.9 as overweight**, and **≥ 30 as obese**. BMI is a useful screening tool but does not distinguish fat from muscle, so it is supplemented by waist circumference and body-composition measures. Treatment rests on creating a sustained **energy deficit** (intake below expenditure). Because roughly **7700 kcal** are stored per kilogram of body fat, a deficit of about **500 kcal/day** predicts roughly **0.45 kg (1 lb) of fat loss per week** — though metabolic adaptation, covered earlier, slows this over time. Newer pharmacotherapies (GLP-1 receptor agonists such as **semaglutide**) and bariatric surgery supplement, but do not replace, dietary management.

**Type-2 diabetes** is a disease of insulin resistance and impaired glucose control. Nutrition therapy centers on **glycemic control**: matching carbohydrate intake to the body's ability to handle glucose. A core skill is **carbohydrate counting**, in which patients quantify the grams of carbohydrate per meal (often in 15 g 'carb choices') to guide food choices and, for those on insulin, to calculate mealtime insulin doses via an **insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio**. Emphasizing **low-glycemic-load** foods, fiber, and consistent meal timing smooths the postprandial glucose response. Long-term control is monitored by **HbA1c (glycated hemoglobin)**, which reflects average blood glucose over roughly three months; the landmark **Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT, 1993)** and the **UK Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS, 1998)** established that tighter glycemic control reduces complications.

**Cardiovascular nutrition** targets the diet-related drivers of heart disease. Reducing **sodium** lowers blood pressure (the DASH and sodium-reduction trials), and managing **blood lipids** — lowering LDL cholesterol and saturated fat while favoring unsaturated fats and omega-3s — reduces atherosclerotic risk, as the Seven Countries Study and decades of trials have shown. The **American Heart Association** and the Dietary Guidelines converge on a pattern rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, fish, and unsaturated oils, with limited sodium, added sugar, and saturated fat — essentially the Mediterranean and DASH patterns. Clinical nutrition thus operationalizes the energy and macronutrient principles of earlier lessons into disease-specific therapy.

slides.title: Sports nutrition: fueling, protein timing, hydration, and ergogenic aids
slides.body:
**Sports nutrition** optimizes intake to support training, performance, and recovery. The joint position stand of the **Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM)** is the authoritative reference.

**Carbohydrate is the master fuel** for moderate-to-high-intensity exercise, stored as muscle and liver **glycogen**. Because glycogen stores are limited (around 500 g, or ~2000 kcal), depleting them causes fatigue ('hitting the wall'). **Carbohydrate loading** — popularized by the Swedish physiologists **Gunvar Ahlborg** and **Jonas Bergström** (whose 1960s muscle-biopsy studies first quantified glycogen) — is the practice of tapering training while eating a high-carbohydrate diet (commonly **8–12 g/kg/day**) in the days before an endurance event to maximize glycogen stores. During prolonged exercise, athletes consume **30–90 g of carbohydrate per hour** to sustain blood glucose.

**Protein** supports muscle repair and adaptation. While the general RDA is 0.8 g/kg/day, athletes need substantially more: current evidence supports **1.6–2.2 g/kg/day** to maximize muscle protein synthesis and lean-mass gains, with research by **Stuart Phillips** at **McMaster University** prominent in establishing these targets. **Protein timing and distribution** matter: spreading intake across the day in **~20–40 g doses** every few hours, including after training and before sleep, supports sustained synthesis. The leucine content of a meal is a key trigger of the synthetic response.

**Hydration** is critical because even mild dehydration (a fluid loss of **~2% of body mass**) impairs endurance and cognition. Athletes are advised to begin exercise well hydrated, drink to limit losses during prolonged efforts, and replace **electrolytes** — chiefly **sodium** — during long events to prevent **hyponatremia** (dangerously low blood sodium from drinking plain water in excess). Sweat-rate testing individualizes fluid plans.

Among **ergogenic aids** (performance supplements), few are well supported, but **creatine monohydrate** is the most evidence-backed. Creatine increases muscle **phosphocreatine** stores, regenerating ATP rapidly during short, intense efforts; a typical protocol is a loading phase (~20 g/day for 5–7 days) followed by ~3–5 g/day maintenance, increasing strength, power, and lean mass. Other supported aids include **caffeine** and **dietary nitrate (beetroot juice)**. The **International Olympic Committee** and **WADA** caution that many supplements are unregulated and may be contaminated with banned substances, so athletes must choose third-party-tested products. Sound sports nutrition thus rests on a foundation of adequate energy, periodized carbohydrate, sufficient and well-timed protein, careful hydration, and a small set of evidence-based supplements.

slides.title: Nutrition support and eating disorders
slides.body:
When patients cannot meet their needs by eating normally, clinical nutrition provides **nutrition support**, and when eating itself is disordered, it requires specialized, multidisciplinary care.

**Nutrition support** is medical feeding, delivered by one of two routes, summarized by the clinical maxim *'if the gut works, use it.'*

- **Enteral nutrition (EN)** delivers liquid formula directly into the functioning GI tract through a tube — a **nasogastric tube** (nose to stomach) for short-term use, or a surgically placed **gastrostomy (PEG)** or **jejunostomy** tube for the long term. EN is preferred whenever the gut is functional because it preserves the integrity of the intestinal lining, maintains the microbiome, costs less, and carries fewer infectious and metabolic complications.
- **Parenteral nutrition (PN)** bypasses the gut entirely, delivering nutrients intravenously. **Total parenteral nutrition (TPN)** supplies a complete formula of amino acids, dextrose, lipid emulsion, electrolytes, vitamins, and trace elements through a central vein. PN is reserved for patients whose gut cannot be used — for example, in short-bowel syndrome, bowel obstruction, or severe pancreatitis. It carries greater risks: catheter-related bloodstream infection, liver complications, and metabolic disturbances.

A critical danger in both routes — and in any reintroduction of food to a severely malnourished patient — is **refeeding syndrome**, first widely recognized in survivors of famine and prisoner-of-war camps after World War II (and informed by the **Minnesota Starvation Experiment**, Ancel Keys, 1944–1945). When carbohydrate is reintroduced, a surge of insulin drives **phosphate, potassium, and magnesium** into cells, causing potentially fatal **hypophosphatemia**, cardiac arrhythmia, and fluid shifts. Prevention requires slow, monitored refeeding, electrolyte correction, and **thiamine** supplementation.

**Eating disorders** are serious psychiatric illnesses with profound nutritional consequences, defined in the **DSM-5** (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). **Anorexia nervosa** involves severe energy restriction, very low body weight, and intense fear of weight gain; it carries the **highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder**, from medical complications and suicide. **Bulimia nervosa** involves cycles of binge eating and compensatory behaviors (self-induced vomiting, laxatives, excessive exercise), which cause electrolyte disturbances (notably **hypokalemia**), dental erosion, and esophageal injury. **Binge-eating disorder**, the most common, involves recurrent binges without regular compensation and is associated with obesity. Nutritional management is delivered by a **multidisciplinary team** — physician, registered dietitian, and mental-health clinician — and focuses on medical stabilization, careful weight restoration (vigilant for refeeding syndrome), normalization of eating patterns, and challenging disordered beliefs about food. Recognizing these conditions, and never treating them as simple matters of willpower, is an essential competency for any nutrition professional.

question.question: A clinician is choosing a route of nutrition support for a patient with a fully functioning gastrointestinal tract who cannot swallow safely after a stroke. Which choice is most appropriate and why?
options: Total parenteral nutrition, because intravenous feeding is always safer than using the gut.

Enteral nutrition via a feeding tube, because when the gut works it is preferred — it preserves intestinal integrity and the microbiome, costs less, and has fewer infectious and metabolic complications than parenteral nutrition.
Parenteral nutrition, because the patient's swallowing problem means the entire gut is non-functional.
No nutrition support is needed; the patient should simply be encouraged to eat more.
question.explanation: The clinical maxim is 'if the gut works, use it.' This patient's GI tract is functional; only swallowing is impaired. Enteral nutrition (e.g., a nasogastric or PEG tube) is therefore preferred because it maintains gut integrity and the microbiome, is cheaper, and has fewer infectious and metabolic complications than parenteral nutrition. Parenteral nutrition is reserved for a non-functional gut. A swallowing impairment does not mean the gut is non-functional, and an unsafe-swallow patient cannot simply eat more by mouth.

hints: Remember the maxim: 'if the gut works, use it.'
The problem is swallowing, not gut function.
slides.workedSolution: Because the gut is functional and only swallowing is impaired, enteral (tube) feeding is preferred over parenteral nutrition — it preserves the gut and microbiome, costs less, and has fewer complications. Parenteral nutrition is for a non-functional gut, which is not the case here.

question.question: A 75 kg endurance athlete is advised to consume 2.0 g of protein per kg of body weight per day to support training adaptation. How many grams of protein should she consume per day?

A client wants to lose body fat. Assuming about 7700 kcal are stored per kilogram of fat, what daily energy deficit (in kcal/day) is needed to lose approximately 0.5 kg of fat per week? Round to the nearest whole number.
Which statement about creatine monohydrate as an ergogenic aid is best supported by evidence?
options: Creatine works mainly by directly building muscle protein, replacing the need for dietary protein.

Creatine increases muscle phosphocreatine stores, enabling faster ATP regeneration during short, high-intensity efforts, and can increase strength, power, and lean mass; a common protocol is a loading phase followed by a maintenance dose.
Creatine is an anabolic steroid banned by WADA for all athletes.
Creatine primarily improves performance in long, low-intensity endurance events by sparing fat.
question.explanation: Creatine monohydrate is among the most evidence-backed supplements. It raises intramuscular phosphocreatine, which regenerates ATP rapidly during short, intense bouts (sprints, lifts), improving strength, power, and lean mass. A typical protocol is loading (~20 g/day for 5–7 days) then ~3–5 g/day maintenance. It is not an anabolic steroid, is not banned by WADA, does not replace dietary protein, and its benefits are for short high-intensity work rather than prolonged low-intensity endurance.

hints: Creatine's mechanism involves the phosphocreatine–ATP system.
Its benefits are greatest for short, powerful efforts, not slow endurance.
slides.workedSolution: Creatine boosts muscle phosphocreatine to speed ATP regeneration during short, intense efforts, increasing strength, power, and lean mass; protocols use a loading then maintenance dose. It is legal (not banned by WADA), is not a steroid, and does not replace protein or primarily aid slow endurance.

question.question: Refeeding a severely malnourished patient
question.prompt: A 19-year-old with severe anorexia nervosa is admitted at a dangerously low body weight after months of minimal intake. The medical team is eager to restore her weight quickly and proposes starting full-calorie feeding immediately. As the dietitian, explain the danger of refeeding syndrome: describe the electrolyte shifts (phosphate, potassium, magnesium) that occur when carbohydrate and insulin surge, why hypophosphatemia is life-threatening, and the role of thiamine. Recommend a safer refeeding approach and explain why aggressive immediate feeding could be harmful or fatal.
